note: Discovery leads for topic workers. Every topic must still research and verify its own sources; nothing here is pre-approved for reuse. An intro-economics survey (micro foundations + market structures + macro + money/banking + international). Accuracy of definitions, model mechanics, and any cited figure is the defining control.

tierA.provider: OpenStax — Principles of Economics / Microeconomics / Macroeconomics
tierA.useFor: authoritative CC BY OER for definitions, models (supply/demand, PPF, market structures, AD/AS), and worked examples
GDP and national-accounts definitions and data
unemployment, CPI/inflation, labor-market definitions and data
monetary policy, interest rates, money supply, banking; FRED for series and definitions

tierB.provider: Federal Reserve Education / regional Fed explainers
tierB.useFor: plain-language explainers of money, banking, the Fed, monetary policy

tierB.provider: International Monetary Fund (IMF) — Finance & Development 'Back to Basics'
tierB.useFor: concise authoritative primers on trade, exchange rates, inflation, GDP

tierB.provider: World Bank / Our World in Data
tierB.useFor: globalization, growth, and trade data (CC BY; attribute; describe, don't reproduce charts)
fiscal policy, government debt/deficits — nonpartisan U.S. source
REFERENCE_ONLY cross-check of definitions; never the sole source for a claim; verify against a Tier A/B source

cautions: POSITIVE vs NORMATIVE is the defining control. Teach positive economics (what is / how models work) as settled where it is settled, and clearly LABEL normative and policy questions (minimum wage, tariffs, tax policy, austerity vs stimulus) as contested. Where schools of thought genuinely disagree (Keynesian, monetarist/classical, supply-side, etc.), present the competing views neutrally and name them — do NOT declare a winner or imply consensus that does not exist.

NO individualized financial, investment, tax, or legal advice. This is general economics education. Do not tell readers what to buy, sell, or how to invest; explain concepts, not personal recommendations.

Every QUANTITATIVE claim must carry a date and an attributable source, and must be verified against it. GDP, unemployment, inflation (CPI), interest rates, debt, and exchange-rate figures move constantly — attribute to BEA/BLS/Fed/Treasury/IMF with the specific period (e.g., 'U.S. unemployment was X% in <month year>, per BLS'). Prefer illustrative/rounded or clearly-dated figures over stale precise ones. Never invent a statistic.

Define terms with textbook precision and guard the classic confusions: demand/supply are whole schedules (curves), not a single 'amount'; distinguish a SHIFT of a curve from a MOVEMENT along it (a price change moves along; a determinant change shifts); nominal vs real (inflation-adjusted); stock vs flow (debt is a stock, deficit is a flow; wealth vs income); quantity demanded vs demand. State model assumptions (ceteris paribus, rational agents, perfect information) and their limits.

Keep MICRO and MACRO distinct. Micro (scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, supply/demand, elasticity, firm costs/production, market structures, externalities, public goods, labor markets) vs macro (GDP, growth, unemployment, inflation, business cycle, AD/AS, fiscal & monetary policy, money/banking/the Fed, debt) vs international (comparative advantage, trade, tariffs, exchange rates, globalization). Each topic owns its slice; name-and-hand-off neighboring topics rather than re-teaching them.

Attribute foundational ideas correctly: opportunity cost and the invisible hand (Adam Smith), comparative advantage (David Ricardo), the general theory / demand-side stabilization (Keynes), the quantity theory / monetarism (Friedman), the tragedy of the commons (Hardin) and its critique (Ostrom), marginal utility (the marginalists). Do not overstate any single figure as the 'inventor' of a broad idea.

Distribute question answer keys EVENLY across A/B/C/D, ensuring at least one C and one D per topic. Verify keys yourself from the file. Vary question stems across topics (avoid a reused 'which best describes X' template) to prevent cross-topic near-duplicate flags.
